Now I have the full picture. The root cause is:

- `bypass: authenticate as unregistered invitee` is skipped when `PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS` is not `true`, so `playwright/.auth/invitee.json` is never created.

In bypass mode they get overwritten with real cookies; in non-bypass mode they remain empty (tests will fail gracefully — unauthenticated — rather than crash with a file-not-found error).

**User:** Let's start back up and sort out what's going on with gitleaks.

**Claude:** Resumed from the blocked commit. Ran `gitleaks protect --staged --config .gitleaks.toml -v` to identify the exact findings. The two flagged lines were in `Program.cs`:

```
options.ClientId = googleOpts.ClientId;       // line 136
options.ClientSecret = googleOpts.ClientSecret; // line 137
```

Root cause: the `dotnet-user-secrets` rule regex `(ClientSecret|ClientId)\s*[:=]\s*["']?[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}` had an optional quote (`["']?`), so it matched variable assignments like `googleOpts.ClientSecret` (22 chars, dots allowed) in addition to actual string literals. The intent was to catch hardcoded credential strings, not property-to-property assignments.

Fix: tightened the regex to require both an opening AND closing quote around the value:

```toml
regex = '''(ClientSecret|ClientId)\s*[:=]\s*["'][A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}["']'''
```

This means only lines where the value is a string literal (e.g. `"ClientSecret": "ABCDEF..."`) trigger the rule. Variable assignments like `options.ClientId = googleOpts.ClientId` no longer match. Real secrets hardcoded as string literals still do.

Verified clean with `gitleaks protect --staged` (no leaks found), then committed all T048–T051 changes plus the gitleaks fix in a single commit (`b875dae`).

# Test Suite Troubleshooting Analysis & Reference Guide

**Committee:** Sarah Chen (Lead SDET), James Wu (Staff Architect), Michelle Park (Senior PM)
**Codebase:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban`, branch `001-us3-invitee-accepts-invitation`

---

## 1. Root Cause Summary

### A. Auth State Setup Problems

**What went wrong:** Two distinct auth-state failures occurred at different levels.

First, the integration test `TestAuthenticationHandler` used `[ThreadStatic]` to store the current user. ASP.NET processes requests on thread-pool threads, so async continuations silently lost the thread-local state — all authenticated tests appeared unauthenticated. This also left `DefaultChallengeScheme` pointing at Google, so unauthenticated test requests triggered real Google OAuth redirects that landed on unroutable URLs.

Second, in Playwright, `auth.setup.ts` lacked an existence guard on `admin.json`. The setup project ran on every `npm run test:e2e:demo` invocation and forced a new Google OAuth session each time, despite the purpose of `storageState` being to reuse a saved session.

Additionally, `ADMIN_EMAIL` defaulted to `'admin@test.local'` but the real seeded admin has the developer's Google email. The dev seed endpoint queried `WHERE admin_email = ADMIN_EMAIL`, found nothing, and returned 404 — silently breaking every test that used the seed endpoint, with an error message that pointed at a trivially-wrong constant rather than the architectural mismatch.

**Why hard to debug:** `[ThreadStatic]` failures are intermittent-looking because they depend on which thread pool thread handles a given request, so the failure signature resembles flakiness. The Google OAuth redirect chase produced misleading 404/500 status codes with no trace of the actual auth misconfiguration. The `admin.json` guard issue wasn't a test failure — it was a usability problem that cost manual sign-in time on every run, burning time before tests even ran.

**Cost:** Sessions 6 and 16 combined. The `[ThreadStatic]` bug cost most of Session 6. The `ADMIN_EMAIL` / setup guard issues cost significant investigation time in Session 16 and required three separate fix iterations before scenario 1 could be tested at all.

---

### B. Locator Strategy Problems

**What went wrong:** Fluent UI's `Title1` component defaults to rendering as a `<span>`, not a heading element. Tests using `getByRole('heading')` found nothing. The fix — `Title1 as="h1"` — is not documented at the call site and is easy to miss because the visual output looks like a heading even when the ARIA role is absent.

In the Playwright e2e tests, scenario 3-6 error messages are located with `getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: /no longer valid|invite\.invalid/i })`. Fluent UI's `MessageBar` with `role="alert"` does expose an alert role, but only because `role="alert"` is applied explicitly in the component source (`AcceptInvitePage.tsx:64,71`). Without the explicit prop, Fluent UI's `MessageBar` would render without an alert role and `getByRole('alert')` would return nothing.

The RTL test for the authenticated-auto-mutation case (`it('authenticated state auto-calls accept mutation with the token')`) mocks `mutate` from the `idleMutation` object but the component was later changed to use `mutateAsync`. The test continued to pass only because both functions were stubbed in `idleMutation` — a coincidence, not a contract. If `mutate` had been removed from the stub, the test would have broken silently with no clear connection to the `mutate → mutateAsync` change.

**Why hard to debug:** Fluent UI wraps HTML elements behind component abstractions. There is no warning when `getByRole('heading')` finds nothing — the test just fails with "unable to find element." The span-rendered `Title1` renders visually correctly, so manual inspection doesn't reveal the problem. The locator works, the page looks right, only the accessibility tree is wrong.

**Cost:** Caught and fixed in Session 9 as part of the SignInPage/NotRegisteredPage implementation (T052/T053), but the pattern recurs anywhere Fluent UI typography components are used without the `as` prop.

---

### C. React Lifecycle + TanStack Query Mutation Timing

**What went wrong:** Two distinct but related failures, both caused by React 18 StrictMode's double-invocation of effects.

**First failure (double-fire of `mutate`):** `AcceptInvitePage` called `mutate(token)` inside a `useEffect` with no guard. StrictMode mounts the component, fires the effect (calls `mutate` — consumes the token successfully), then immediately fakes an unmount and remounts, firing the effect again. The second `mutate(token)` hit the API with an already-consumed token and returned 410. The component showed the "no longer valid" error. The Playwright test timed out at `/accept/<token>`.

Fix: `useRef(false)` guard (`hasAttempted`). `useRef` survives StrictMode's fake unmount while mutation state (`data`, `error`, `isPending`) does not. The guard was set to `true` on first attempt and checked on every effect re-invocation.

**Second failure (`mutate` vs `mutateAsync` — TanStack Query observer lifecycle):** After adding the `hasAttempted` guard, the test still timed out. The API was returning 200 (confirmed by adding `page.on('response')` diagnostic logging), but `navigate('/')` never fired.

Root cause: StrictMode's fake unmount destroys the TanStack Query `MutationObserver` that tracks `data/error/isPending`. The mutation from the first mount resolves and notifies the destroyed observer — the remounted component's fresh observer starts with `data = undefined`. The `useEffect([data, navigate])` watcher never sees `data` become non-undefined, so `navigate('/')` is never called.

Fix: Replace `mutate(token)` + `useEffect([data, navigate])` with `mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})`. Promise `.then()` callbacks are not tied to React's observer lifecycle — they fire when the Promise resolves regardless of remounting. `navigate` from `useNavigate()` is stable across remounts in React Router v6.

**Why hard to debug:** Both failures produced the same symptom (page stays at `/accept/<token>`), disguising them as the same bug. The first fix (hasAttempted) removed one failure mode but revealed a second with identical symptoms. The second failure was invisible without the `page.on('response')` diagnostic because there was no console error — the mutation resolved successfully, the result was simply lost. This is a known TanStack Query + StrictMode interaction but the diagnosis requires understanding both React's fake-unmount cycle and TanStack Query's internal observer model simultaneously.

**Cost:** This occupied all of Sessions 16 and 17 and spanned multiple agent context windows. It accounts for the majority of the total troubleshooting overhead across all sessions.

---

### D. Async Timing / waitFor Strategy

**What went wrong:** The RTL test for "success navigates to home" used `waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('Home Page')).toBeInTheDocument())`. This works when the component navigates imperatively, but the test setup mocked `useAcceptInvite` to return a success state directly (bypassing the mutation flow entirely). The component's navigation logic ran during initial render rather than as an async response to mutation completion. This is functionally correct but tests a different code path than what runs in production.

In Playwright, scenario 1 used a 15-second `toHaveURL` timeout. This is appropriate for an async navigation but was not enough to surface that the underlying mutation was succeeding but the navigate was not being called — the error message said "timeout" but the root cause was a missing effect dependency, not a slow operation.

**Why hard to debug:** RTL tests with fully-mocked hooks don't exercise the async mutation lifecycle at all. They verify rendering given a state, not the state transitions. The mock for "success navigates to home" pre-loads the success state rather than simulating the mutation resolving — so the `mutateAsync → .then(navigate)` code path was never exercised by RTL. The Playwright test was the only test that caught this.

**Cost:** The mismatch between what RTL tests verify and what Playwright tests verify is why the RTL suite was green while Playwright failed. Each session invested in debugging what RTL had already "proven" was working.

---

### E. Test Isolation: Rate Limiters, Shared DB State, Concurrent Tests

**What went wrong:** Three distinct isolation failures.

**Rate limiter in integration tests:** The concurrent-acceptance integration test sent 20 simultaneous requests. The `anonymous` rate limiter in Program.cs was configured as a global (not per-IP) fixed-window limiter with `PermitLimit = 10`. All 20 requests competed for the same 10-slot bucket. Approximately 10 requests were rejected with 429 before reaching the SQLite layer. The test assertion only checked for 200 and 410 — the 429s showed up as the unexplained shortfall. The test appeared to verify DB concurrency semantics but was actually testing rate limiter throughput.

Fix: Two changes — (1) fix the global → per-IP partitioned rate limiter in `Program.cs` (this was also a production bug), and (2) `KanbanWebAppFactory` overrides rate limiter options with `PermitLimit = 10_000` so integration test correctness is not contingent on rate limiter configuration.

**SQLite BUSY under concurrency:** With 20 concurrent requests all hitting the same deferred-transaction pattern, requests that couldn't acquire the write lock retried under Polly. With only 3 retries at 50ms/100ms/200ms backoff, retry exhaustion was possible before the first writer committed. Fixes: `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` (SQLite waits internally before surfacing SQLITE_BUSY to .NET), `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` (allows concurrent reads + one writer, reducing lock contention), and Polly retries bumped to 20 with jitter.

**FK constraint ordering:** SQLite 10.0.8 enforces FK constraints by default. The original `TryConsumeAsync` set `consumed_by_user_id = newUserId` before the user row existed, producing `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. This was not a test isolation problem per se, but it revealed that the DB schema constraint behavior had changed silently between versions and the test suite was not designed to catch this class of schema enforcement change.

**Why hard to debug:** The rate limiter failure produced 429 responses that the test assertion didn't check for, so the assertion printed "expected 19 Gone, got 4 Gone" with no mention of 429. The SQLITE_BUSY failure was non-deterministic (number of 410s varied run-to-run) which initially pointed away from a systematic cause. The FK failure was deterministic but the error (`FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` → 500) looked like a different problem from the concurrency issue.

**Cost:** Session 14 entirely. The Polly + rate limiter + WAL fix chain spanned multiple agent loops within the session.

---

### F. Component Design That Made Testing Harder

**What went wrong:** `AcceptInvitePage` combines three concerns in one component:
1. Authentication state check (`isUnauthenticated` from `useCurrentUser`)
2. Auto-mutation trigger (the `useEffect` that calls `mutateAsync`)
3. Error/success rendering

The authentication check and the mutation trigger were coupled in the same `useEffect`:

```typescript
useEffect(() => {
  if (hasAttempted.current) return
  if (!isUnauthenticated && token) {
    hasAttempted.current = true
    mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})
  }
}, [isUnauthenticated, token, mutateAsync, navigate])
```

This means: the auth-check logic and the mutation-invocation logic are not independently testable. To test "authenticated user auto-calls mutation," you must mock both `useCurrentUser` and `useAcceptInvite` simultaneously, and the test verifies the interaction between the effect guard, the auth check, and the mutation invocation as a single unit — a behavior that lives nowhere explicitly in the code.

The RTL tests responded to this by mocking `mutate` (not `mutateAsync`) in the `idleMutation` stub, because at the time the tests were written `mutate` was the API. When the component switched to `mutateAsync`, the tests continued to pass because both were in the stub — masking the contract change.

The deeper issue: the component's observable contract from a test perspective is "fires the mutation when authenticated and not yet attempted." But the test verifies `mockMutate.toHaveBeenCalledWith('myspecialtoken')` — an implementation detail (which function was called) rather than the observable behavior (the API request was made). The Playwright test is more contract-oriented: it verifies the navigation happened, which is the true externally-observable outcome.

**Why hard to debug:** When `mutate` was replaced by `mutateAsync`, the RTL tests didn't break. The tests gave false confidence that the component was correct. The Playwright test caught the actual failure, but by then the RTL "evidence" had already consumed debugging time eliminating component logic as the cause.

**Cost:** This design contributed to every session from 16 onwards. The false-green RTL tests directed debugging attention away from the component's async state management and toward infrastructure (seed endpoint, auth state, API responses).

## 2. Reference Guide: Writing Playwright + RTL Tests for This Stack

---

### Rule 1: Always render Fluent UI typography with `as="h1/h2/..."` to get ARIA roles
**Anti-pattern:**
```tsx
<Title1>Accept Invitation</Title1>  // renders as <span> — no heading role
```
**Pattern:**
```tsx
<Title1 as="h1">Accept Invitation</Title1>  // renders as <h1> — getByRole('heading') works
```
**Why:** Fluent UI `Title1`, `Title2`, `Body1`, etc. default to `<span>` elements. `getByRole('heading')` finds nothing. Visual output is identical; only the accessibility tree differs. WCAG 2.1 AA requires proper heading structure regardless.

**Applies to:** All Fluent UI typography components in the codebase. Verify with `getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })` in every component test — if it fails with no other obvious reason, check the `as` prop.

---

### Rule 2: Explicitly apply `role="alert"` to Fluent UI MessageBar for ARIA-based locators
**Anti-pattern:**
```tsx
<MessageBar intent="error">...</MessageBar>  // no alert role exposed to ARIA tree
```
**Pattern:**
```tsx
<MessageBar intent="error" role="alert">...</MessageBar>
```
**Why:** Fluent UI `MessageBar` does not automatically set `role="alert"`. Without it, `getByRole('alert')` and `page.getByRole('alert')` return nothing. The Playwright tests' `filter({ hasText: ... })` chain only works because the explicit prop is in place. This is both a testability requirement and an accessibility requirement (live regions must be announced to screen readers).

---

### Rule 3: In RTL, mock at the hook boundary, not the fetch boundary — but verify the contract, not the implementation
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Verifies implementation detail — breaks when mutate → mutateAsync
const mockMutate = vi.fn()
mockUseAcceptInvite.mockReturnValue({ ...idleMutation, mutate: mockMutate })
// ...
expect(mockMutate).toHaveBeenCalledWith('myspecialtoken')
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
// Verifies observable contract — survives internal refactoring
const mockMutateAsync = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(acceptResponse)
mockUseAcceptInvite.mockReturnValue({ ...idleMutation, mutateAsync: mockMutateAsync })
// ...
await waitFor(() => expect(mockMutateAsync).toHaveBeenCalledWith('myspecialtoken'))
// Better yet: verify the downstream effect
await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('Home Page')).toBeInTheDocument())
```
**Why:** Component contracts are defined by what the component does (navigates to `/`), not how it does it (calls `mutate` vs `mutateAsync`). When you mock at the hook boundary but assert on internal function calls, any refactoring of the hook's API surface breaks tests without breaking behavior. The RTL "auto-calls mutation" test should assert that `navigate('/')` was called, or that the home page renders — not which function the component invoked.

---

### Rule 4: Never use `mutate` when the component needs to chain on the result; always use `mutateAsync`
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// mutate result is only available through TanStack Query's observer —
// destroyed on StrictMode fake-unmount
mutate(token)
// separate effect watching data — never fires if observer was destroyed
useEffect(() => {
  if (data) navigate('/')
}, [data, navigate])
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
// Promise chain is not tied to React observer lifecycle
mutateAsync(token)
  .then(() => navigate('/'))
  .catch(() => {}) // error already in mutation state for render
```
**Why:** React 18 StrictMode intentionally fakes an unmount+remount cycle. TanStack Query's `MutationObserver` is destroyed on the fake unmount. When the mutation resolves, it notifies the destroyed observer — the remounted component's fresh observer never receives the result. Promise `.then()` callbacks fire when the Promise resolves regardless of component lifecycle. `navigate` from React Router v6 is a stable reference that is safe to call from outside the component's effect tree.

**Rule of thumb:** Use `mutate` for fire-and-forget mutations where the UI reads state from `data`/`error` on re-render. Use `mutateAsync` when you need to chain imperative logic (navigation, conditional redirect, cascading mutation) on the mutation result.

---

### Rule 5: Always guard auto-firing `useEffect` mutations with `useRef` to survive StrictMode
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
useEffect(() => {
  mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/'))
}, [token, mutateAsync, navigate])
// Fires twice in StrictMode — second call hits already-consumed token
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
const hasAttempted = useRef(false)

useEffect(() => {
  if (hasAttempted.current) return
  if (!isUnauthenticated && token) {
    hasAttempted.current = true
    mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})
  }
}, [isUnauthenticated, token, mutateAsync, navigate])
```
**Why:** `useRef` survives StrictMode's fake unmount while state variables, `useState`, and TanStack Query mutation state do not. The guard prevents the second StrictMode effect invocation from making a second API call. Without it, one-time operations (invitation acceptance, payment processing, any idempotent-by-design endpoint) fire twice in development, consuming the resource before the success path can run.

**Important caveat:** This pattern is necessary in production code because StrictMode behavior in development mirrors unmount/remount patterns that occur legitimately in production (e.g., React Suspense boundaries, concurrent rendering). Don't disable StrictMode to avoid the issue — fix the effect.

---

### Rule 6: Auth state setup — the dev authenticate endpoint is always required for test users
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Assumes INVITEE_EMAIL can use Google OAuth
setup('authenticate as invitee', async ({ page }) => {
  setup.skip(!BYPASS, 'bypass path only')
  await page.goto(`${API_BASE}/api/v1/dev/authenticate?email=...`)
})
// Result: invitee.json is never written in demo mode
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
setup('authenticate as unregistered invitee', async ({ page }) => {
  // No Google sign-in path exists for test invitees — dev endpoint is the only option
  // regardless of whether PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS is set.
  await page.goto(`${API_BASE}/api/v1/dev/authenticate?email=${encodeURIComponent(INVITEE_EMAIL)}`)
  await page.waitForURL(`${WEB_BASE}/**`)
  await page.context().storageState({ path: INVITEE_AUTH })
})
```
**Why:** The Google OAuth path is only available for users who have real Google accounts and are added as test users in the Google Cloud Console. Test invitees and unregistered users are synthetic — they exist only in the test DB. There is no Google sign-in path for them. The dev authenticate endpoint is always the right tool for these personas, regardless of `PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS`. Only the admin setup test has a real-Google path; all other personas use the dev endpoint exclusively.

---

### Rule 7: Guard storageState setup with an existence check to avoid forced re-auth
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
setup('google: authenticate as admin', async ({ page, context }) => {
  setup.skip(BYPASS, 'real Google path only')
  // No existence check — forces re-auth on every demo run
  await page.goto(`${WEB_BASE}/signin`)
  // ... Google sign-in ...
  await context.storageState({ path: ADMIN_AUTH })
})
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
setup('google: authenticate as admin', async ({ page, context }) => {
  setup.skip(BYPASS, 'real Google path only')
  setup.skip(
    fs.existsSync(ADMIN_AUTH),
    'saved session exists — delete playwright/.auth/admin.json to force re-auth'
  )
  setup.setTimeout(180_000)
  // ... Google sign-in ...
  await context.storageState({ path: ADMIN_AUTH })
})
```
**Why:** The `setup` project runs as a dependency before every `chromium` project run. Without the existence guard, every `npm run test:e2e:demo` forces a new Google sign-in even when the saved session is still valid (Google sessions last weeks). This is a friction cost on every test run that is entirely avoidable.

---

### Rule 8: Dev seed endpoint admin lookup must use `system_role` not email
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Falls apart when admin email is the developer's real Google address
data: { adminEmail: ADMIN_EMAIL }
// ...endpoint queries by email, but ADMIN_EMAIL = 'admin@test.local' default
```
**Pattern:**
```sql
SELECT id FROM users WHERE system_role = 'Admin' LIMIT 1
```
**Why:** The seeded admin user has whatever email the developer configured in `Seed:AdminEmail` user secrets. A constant in `auth.helpers.ts` pointing to `'admin@test.local'` will never match the real seeded admin. The dev seed endpoint should discover the admin dynamically by role. Note SQLite's case-sensitive `=` operator: `'Admin'` (Pascal case, matching the migration) not `'admin'`.

---

### Rule 9: Integration test infrastructure must neutralize rate limiters
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Integration tests run against production rate limiter configuration
// 20 concurrent requests → 10 rejected with 429 → test appears to fail for wrong reason
```
**Pattern:**
```csharp
// KanbanWebAppFactory.ConfigureServices:
services.RemoveAll(typeof(IConfigureOptions<RateLimiterOptions>));
services.AddRateLimiter(opts => {
    opts.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;
    opts.AddFixedWindowLimiter("anonymous", o => { o.PermitLimit = 10_000; o.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1); });
    opts.AddSlidingWindowLimiter("authenticated", o => { o.PermitLimit = 10_000; ... });
    opts.AddSlidingWindowLimiter("mutating", o => { o.PermitLimit = 10_000; ... });
});
```
**Why:** Integration tests that exercise concurrency semantics must not have their behavior shaped by rate limiting. The test for concurrent acceptance is verifying DB-level `consumed_at IS NULL` atomicity — it should not be constrained by a 10-request/minute bucket. This is a general rule: integration tests should disable or vastly raise all infrastructure limits (rate limiter, retry budgets, timeouts) that are not themselves the subject of the test.

**Important:** Every named policy in `Program.cs` must also appear in the factory override. A missing policy causes a runtime error on any endpoint using `.RequireRateLimiting`. Add a maintenance comment to this effect in the factory.

---

### Rule 10: Component test idleMutation stub must include both `mutate` and `mutateAsync`
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
const idleMutation = {
  mutate: vi.fn(),
  // mutateAsync omitted — test breaks silently if component switches to mutateAsync
  data: undefined, error: null, isPending: false, ...
}
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
const idleMutation = {
  mutate: vi.fn(),
  mutateAsync: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  data: undefined, error: null, isPending: false,
  isIdle: true, isSuccess: false, isError: false,
  variables: undefined, context: undefined,
  failureCount: 0, failureReason: null, isPaused: false,
  status: 'idle' as const, submittedAt: 0, reset: vi.fn(),
}
```
**Why:** The full TanStack Query mutation return type includes both. If the component uses `mutateAsync` and the test only provides `mutate`, the component calls `undefined()` and throws. TypeScript should catch this — which means the test fixture's type annotation should be `UseMutationResult<TData, TError, TVariables>`, not an inline object literal with inferred type.

---

### Rule 11: For Playwright async assertions, use `waitForResponse` to separate API timing from UI timing
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Conflates "API call succeeded" with "navigation happened"
// Timeout message says nothing about whether the API even responded
await expect(page).toHaveURL(`${WEB_BASE}/`, { timeout: 15_000 })
```
**Pattern (for debugging; remove after fix):**
```typescript
const [acceptResponse] = await Promise.all([
  page.waitForResponse(resp => resp.url().includes('/invites/') && resp.url().endsWith('/accept')),
  page.goto(`${WEB_BASE}/accept/${token}`)
])
expect(acceptResponse.status()).toBe(200)
await expect(page).toHaveURL(`${WEB_BASE}/`, { timeout: 5_000 })
```
**Why:** `toHaveURL` timeout tells you the navigation never happened, but not why. `waitForResponse` separates the question "did the API call succeed?" from "did the navigation happen?" When these are separate, you immediately know whether the problem is in the API or in the component's response to the API. This is the diagnostic pattern used in Session 17 (`page.on('response')`) — make it the default for any test where an API call triggers a navigation.

---

### Rule 12: Test the component contract at the integration level in Playwright; test the rendering contract at the unit level in RTL
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// RTL test verifies that the component calls mutate when certain state is present.
// Playwright test also verifies the same thing by checking navigation.
// → Two tests, same coverage, different failure modes, one is less trustworthy.
```
**Pattern:**
- **RTL:** Verifies rendering — "given this auth state, renders this button"; "given this error state, renders this message." Does not exercise the mutation lifecycle.
- **Playwright:** Verifies the full user journey — "user lands on /accept/token, API is called, user is navigated to /." This is the only test that exercises the `mutateAsync → .then(navigate)` path end-to-end.

**Why:** RTL with mocked hooks cannot test async mutation lifecycle (StrictMode double-fire, observer destruction on remount) because the lifecycle itself is mocked away. Playwright exercises the real component in a real browser with real React lifecycle. Don't try to duplicate Playwright's coverage in RTL — you will either mock too much (losing the value) or not enough (fighting React internals in jsdom).

**Concrete implication:** The RTL "on successful acceptance navigates to home" test is valuable for verifying that the component renders the home page when mutation state is `isSuccess: true`, but it cannot and should not try to verify that `mutateAsync` is called, returns a promise, and chains to `navigate`. Let Playwright own that.

**Proposed addition after the existing "Four test layers are required" table:**

> **Integration test infrastructure isolation (non-negotiable):**

> - Named rate limiter policies registered in `Program.cs` MUST have corresponding permissive overrides in `KanbanWebAppFactory`. A missing policy override causes runtime errors on endpoints using `.RequireRateLimiting` — the factory MUST include a maintenance comment listing all policies requiring override.

### 3.3 Add "React StrictMode and One-Shot Mutations" to the Frontend State Management section

**Proposed addition after the "Mutation Pattern" subsection:**

> **StrictMode and one-shot mutations (non-negotiable):**
> - React 18 StrictMode intentionally invokes effects twice in development (mount → fake-unmount → remount). Effects that fire `mutate()` or `mutateAsync()` for one-shot operations (invitation acceptance, payment, any endpoint that consumes a single-use resource) MUST be guarded with a `useRef(false)` guard (`hasAttempted` pattern). `useRef` survives StrictMode's fake unmount; mutation state does not.
> - When a mutation result must drive imperative navigation or a cascading action, MUST use `mutateAsync` (returns a Promise) rather than `mutate` (result only available through TanStack Query's observer). The `MutationObserver` is destroyed on StrictMode's fake unmount; a Promise chain is not. Pattern: `mutateAsync(arg).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})`.

**Proposed addition in the E2E Playwright row:**

> - The real-Google setup test MUST include an existence guard (`fs.existsSync(ADMIN_AUTH)`) to skip re-auth when a valid session file exists. Delete `playwright/.auth/admin.json` to force re-auth.
> - The dev authenticate endpoint (`GET /api/v1/dev/authenticate`) is registered only in `IsDevelopment()`. Tests MUST NOT depend on it in a configuration that could run against a non-development environment.
> - `ADMIN_EMAIL` in test helpers MUST be documented as requiring the same value as `Seed:AdminEmail` user secret. Do not default to a synthetic address; instead, the dev seed endpoint MUST discover the admin by `system_role = 'Admin'` query, not by email constant.

### 3.5 Add a "Component Contract Testing" note to Section II — TDD (Fluent UI component test tiers)

**Proposed addition to the Fluent UI component test tiers decision tree:**

> **Tier boundary rule (prevents false-green coverage):**
> - RTL component tests verify **rendering given state**: given `isError: true` and `error.status: 410`, renders the correct `MessageBar`. They MUST mock hooks at the module boundary and assert on rendered output, not on which internal function was called.
> - RTL component tests MUST NOT attempt to verify async mutation lifecycle (StrictMode double-fire, observer destruction, Promise chaining). This lifecycle can only be verified in a real browser environment — use Playwright for this.

## 4. PM Perspective: Signal vs Noise

### Which failures were "preventable noise" vs "valuable signal"

**Preventable noise (should never have reached debugging):**

- `[ThreadStatic]` in `TestAuthenticationHandler` — this is a known threading anti-pattern in any async .NET context. A constitution rule specifying "test authentication handlers MUST use thread-safe state storage" would have prevented one full session.
- `ADMIN_EMAIL = 'admin@test.local'` constant mismatch — this is a configuration coupling problem. The seed endpoint should never have accepted an email parameter at all; the admin should always be discovered by role.
- `auth.setup.ts` missing the `fs.existsSync` guard — this is a known Playwright setup pattern that appears in the official docs. Cost: multiple forced re-auths and session overhead.
- StrictMode double-fire without the `hasAttempted` guard — React's own documentation describes this behavior and the ref guard pattern. This is a well-known React 18 issue with a documented solution.

**Valuable signal (these failures caught real problems):**

- Rate limiter being global instead of per-IP — the integration test's concurrency failure revealed a genuine production bug. Without a 20-concurrent-request test, this would have been invisible until production traffic hit the limit.
- FK constraint enforcement change in `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite 10.0.8` — the test correctly caught that the `TryConsumeAsync` implementation had an ordering bug that was only harmless because FK enforcement was historically off by default.
- `google.missing_sub` error during real Google setup — this caught a real claim-name remapping bug in `GoogleIdentityAdapter` that would have broken every production sign-in.
- `mutateAsync` observer destruction on remount — this is a genuine React + TanStack Query interaction that the Playwright test correctly identified as broken behavior. The RTL suite was green, which gave false confidence.

**Summary:** Approximately 60% of the debugging time in Sessions 14-17 was spent on preventable noise (configuration mismatches, known framework patterns, threading anti-patterns). The remaining 40% was valuable signal that caught real production bugs.

---

### What the team should do differently at the test planning phase

**1. Write the auth setup matrix before writing any tests.**
The current `auth.helpers.ts` has three personas but the rules governing which path each persona takes (real Google vs dev endpoint, bypass-conditional vs always-dev-endpoint) are implicit. Before writing a single test, produce a table:

| Persona | Real Google path? | Bypass path? | Dev endpoint required? | Notes |
|---------|------------------|--------------|----------------------|-------|
| Admin | Yes (one-time setup) | Yes (CI) | No | Existence-guarded |
| Invitee | No | Bypass only | Always | No Google identity |
| Unregistered | No | Bypass only | Always | No Google identity |

Any deviation from this table during test writing is a red flag that requires explicit justification.

**2. Document the StrictMode contract for every component that uses `useEffect` with an API call.**
This is a one-line comment: `// One-shot: guarded by hasAttempted ref to survive StrictMode double-invoke`. Its absence in a new component is a code review trigger, not a debugging exercise.

**3. Classify component tests by what they can and cannot verify.**
RTL tests should be labelled with what they prove ("renders error state given 410 error") and what they don't prove ("does not verify that the mutation is invoked from the correct lifecycle hook"). This prevents false confidence from green RTL results when Playwright is failing.

---

### How to write acceptance criteria that make test locator choices obvious

The US3 acceptance scenarios in the spec (`specs/001-auth-onboarding/spec.md`) describe outcomes at the user-visible level but don't specify the ARIA contract. Acceptance criteria should include:

**Instead of:**
> Scenario 3 — expired token shows invitation-no-longer-valid error

**Write:**
> Scenario 3 — expired token: the page displays an error message with text matching "no longer valid" in a region with `role="alert"`. The URL remains at `/accept/<token>`. No navigation occurs.

**Instead of:**
> Scenario 1 — valid token with matching email creates registered user

**Write:**
> Scenario 1 — valid token: after Google authentication, the page auto-submits the acceptance. On success, the browser navigates to `/` within 15 seconds. The main landmark (`role="main"`) becomes visible. No user interaction is required.

This level of specificity in acceptance criteria serves three purposes: (1) it makes the Playwright locator choices deterministic — `getByRole('alert')` vs `getByText(...)` is obvious from the criterion, (2) it surfaces ARIA requirements at story-writing time rather than at code-review time, and (3) it makes the failure message from a failed assertion directly map to the acceptance criterion, reducing diagnosis time.

The guiding principle: acceptance criteria should name the ARIA role or semantic element that will be used to verify each criterion. "The error message is visible" is ambiguous. "An alert region containing 'no longer valid' is visible" is a test.</result>

## 1. Root Cause Summary

### A. Auth State Setup Problems

**What went wrong:** Two distinct auth-state failures occurred at different levels.

First, the integration test `TestAuthenticationHandler` used `[ThreadStatic]` to store the current user. ASP.NET processes requests on thread-pool threads, so async continuations silently lost the thread-local state — all authenticated tests appeared unauthenticated. This also left `DefaultChallengeScheme` pointing at Google, so unauthenticated test requests triggered real Google OAuth redirects that landed on unroutable URLs.

Second, in Playwright, `auth.setup.ts` lacked an existence guard on `admin.json`. The setup project ran on every `npm run test:e2e:demo` invocation and forced a new Google OAuth session each time, despite the purpose of `storageState` being to reuse a saved session.

Additionally, `ADMIN_EMAIL` defaulted to `'admin@test.local'` but the real seeded admin has the developer's Google email. The dev seed endpoint queried `WHERE admin_email = ADMIN_EMAIL`, found nothing, and returned 404 — silently breaking every test that used the seed endpoint, with an error message that pointed at a trivially-wrong constant rather than the architectural mismatch.

**Why hard to debug:** `[ThreadStatic]` failures are intermittent-looking because they depend on which thread pool thread handles a given request, so the failure signature resembles flakiness. The Google OAuth redirect chase produced misleading 404/500 status codes with no trace of the actual auth misconfiguration. The `admin.json` guard issue wasn't a test failure — it was a usability problem that cost manual sign-in time on every run, burning time before tests even ran.

**Cost:** Sessions 6 and 16 combined. The `[ThreadStatic]` bug cost most of Session 6. The `ADMIN_EMAIL` / setup guard issues cost significant investigation time in Session 16 and required three separate fix iterations before scenario 1 could be tested at all.

---

### B. Locator Strategy Problems

**What went wrong:** Fluent UI's `Title1` component defaults to rendering as a `<span>`, not a heading element. Tests using `getByRole('heading')` found nothing. The fix — `Title1 as="h1"` — is not documented at the call site and is easy to miss because the visual output looks like a heading even when the ARIA role is absent.

In the Playwright e2e tests, scenario 3-6 error messages are located with `getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: /no longer valid|invite\.invalid/i })`. Fluent UI's `MessageBar` with `role="alert"` does expose an alert role, but only because `role="alert"` is applied explicitly in the component source (`AcceptInvitePage.tsx:64,71`). Without the explicit prop, Fluent UI's `MessageBar` would render without an alert role and `getByRole('alert')` would return nothing.

The RTL test for the authenticated-auto-mutation case (`it('authenticated state auto-calls accept mutation with the token')`) mocks `mutate` from the `idleMutation` object but the component was later changed to use `mutateAsync`. The test continued to pass only because both functions were stubbed in `idleMutation` — a coincidence, not a contract. If `mutate` had been removed from the stub, the test would have broken silently with no clear connection to the `mutate → mutateAsync` change.

**Why hard to debug:** Fluent UI wraps HTML elements behind component abstractions. There is no warning when `getByRole('heading')` finds nothing — the test just fails with "unable to find element." The span-rendered `Title1` renders visually correctly, so manual inspection doesn't reveal the problem. The locator works, the page looks right, only the accessibility tree is wrong.

**Cost:** Caught and fixed in Session 9 as part of the SignInPage/NotRegisteredPage implementation (T052/T053), but the pattern recurs anywhere Fluent UI typography components are used without the `as` prop.

---

### C. React Lifecycle + TanStack Query Mutation Timing

**What went wrong:** Two distinct but related failures, both caused by React 18 StrictMode's double-invocation of effects.

**First failure (double-fire of `mutate`):** `AcceptInvitePage` called `mutate(token)` inside a `useEffect` with no guard. StrictMode mounts the component, fires the effect (calls `mutate` — consumes the token successfully), then immediately fakes an unmount and remounts, firing the effect again. The second `mutate(token)` hit the API with an already-consumed token and returned 410. The component showed the "no longer valid" error. The Playwright test timed out at `/accept/<token>`.

Fix: `useRef(false)` guard (`hasAttempted`). `useRef` survives StrictMode's fake unmount while mutation state (`data`, `error`, `isPending`) does not. The guard was set to `true` on first attempt and checked on every effect re-invocation.

**Second failure (`mutate` vs `mutateAsync` — TanStack Query observer lifecycle):** After adding the `hasAttempted` guard, the test still timed out. The API was returning 200 (confirmed by adding `page.on('response')` diagnostic logging), but `navigate('/')` never fired.

Root cause: StrictMode's fake unmount destroys the TanStack Query `MutationObserver` that tracks `data/error/isPending`. The mutation from the first mount resolves and notifies the destroyed observer — the remounted component's fresh observer starts with `data = undefined`. The `useEffect([data, navigate])` watcher never sees `data` become non-undefined, so `navigate('/')` is never called.

Fix: Replace `mutate(token)` + `useEffect([data, navigate])` with `mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})`. Promise `.then()` callbacks are not tied to React's observer lifecycle — they fire when the Promise resolves regardless of remounting. `navigate` from `useNavigate()` is stable across remounts in React Router v6.

**Why hard to debug:** Both failures produced the same symptom (page stays at `/accept/<token>`), disguising them as the same bug. The first fix (hasAttempted) removed one failure mode but revealed a second with identical symptoms. The second failure was invisible without the `page.on('response')` diagnostic because there was no console error — the mutation resolved successfully, the result was simply lost. This is a known TanStack Query + StrictMode interaction but the diagnosis requires understanding both React's fake-unmount cycle and TanStack Query's internal observer model simultaneously.

**Cost:** This occupied all of Sessions 16 and 17 and spanned multiple agent context windows. It accounts for the majority of the total troubleshooting overhead across all sessions.

### D. Async Timing / waitFor Strategy

**What went wrong:** The RTL test for "success navigates to home" used `waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('Home Page')).toBeInTheDocument())`. This works when the component navigates imperatively, but the test setup mocked `useAcceptInvite` to return a success state directly (bypassing the mutation flow entirely). The component's navigation logic ran during initial render rather than as an async response to mutation completion. This is functionally correct but tests a different code path than what runs in production.

In Playwright, scenario 1 used a 15-second `toHaveURL` timeout. This is appropriate for an async navigation but was not enough to surface that the underlying mutation was succeeding but the navigate was not being called — the error message said "timeout" but the root cause was a missing effect dependency, not a slow operation.

**Why hard to debug:** RTL tests with fully-mocked hooks don't exercise the async mutation lifecycle at all. They verify rendering given a state, not the state transitions. The mock for "success navigates to home" pre-loads the success state rather than simulating the mutation resolving — so the `mutateAsync → .then(navigate)` code path was never exercised by RTL. The Playwright test was the only test that caught this.

**Cost:** The mismatch between what RTL tests verify and what Playwright tests verify is why the RTL suite was green while Playwright failed. Each session invested in debugging what RTL had already "proven" was working.

### E. Test Isolation: Rate Limiters, Shared DB State, Concurrent Tests

**What went wrong:** Three distinct isolation failures.

**Rate limiter in integration tests:** The concurrent-acceptance integration test sent 20 simultaneous requests. The `anonymous` rate limiter in Program.cs was configured as a global (not per-IP) fixed-window limiter with `PermitLimit = 10`. All 20 requests competed for the same 10-slot bucket. Approximately 10 requests were rejected with 429 before reaching the SQLite layer. The test assertion only checked for 200 and 410 — the 429s showed up as the unexplained shortfall. The test appeared to verify DB concurrency semantics but was actually testing rate limiter throughput.

Fix: Two changes — (1) fix the global → per-IP partitioned rate limiter in `Program.cs` (this was also a production bug), and (2) `KanbanWebAppFactory` overrides rate limiter options with `PermitLimit = 10_000` so integration test correctness is not contingent on rate limiter configuration.

**SQLite BUSY under concurrency:** With 20 concurrent requests all hitting the same deferred-transaction pattern, requests that couldn't acquire the write lock retried under Polly. With only 3 retries at 50ms/100ms/200ms backoff, retry exhaustion was possible before the first writer committed. Fixes: `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` (SQLite waits internally before surfacing SQLITE_BUSY to .NET), `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` (allows concurrent reads + one writer, reducing lock contention), and Polly retries bumped to 20 with jitter.

**FK constraint ordering:** SQLite 10.0.8 enforces FK constraints by default. The original `TryConsumeAsync` set `consumed_by_user_id = newUserId` before the user row existed, producing `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. This was not a test isolation problem per se, but it revealed that the DB schema constraint behavior had changed silently between versions and the test suite was not designed to catch this class of schema enforcement change.

**Why hard to debug:** The rate limiter failure produced 429 responses that the test assertion didn't check for, so the assertion printed "expected 19 Gone, got 4 Gone" with no mention of 429. The SQLITE_BUSY failure was non-deterministic (number of 410s varied run-to-run) which initially pointed away from a systematic cause. The FK failure was deterministic but the error (`FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` → 500) looked like a different problem from the concurrency issue.

**Cost:** Session 14 entirely. The Polly + rate limiter + WAL fix chain spanned multiple agent loops within the session.

### F. Component Design That Made Testing Harder

**What went wrong:** `AcceptInvitePage` combines three concerns in one component:
1. Authentication state check (`isUnauthenticated` from `useCurrentUser`)
2. Auto-mutation trigger (the `useEffect` that calls `mutateAsync`)
3. Error/success rendering

The authentication check and the mutation trigger were coupled in the same `useEffect`:

```typescript
useEffect(() => {
  if (hasAttempted.current) return
  if (!isUnauthenticated && token) {
    hasAttempted.current = true
    mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})
  }
}, [isUnauthenticated, token, mutateAsync, navigate])
```

This means: the auth-check logic and the mutation-invocation logic are not independently testable. To test "authenticated user auto-calls mutation," you must mock both `useCurrentUser` and `useAcceptInvite` simultaneously, and the test verifies the interaction between the effect guard, the auth check, and the mutation invocation as a single unit — a behavior that lives nowhere explicitly in the code.

The RTL tests responded to this by mocking `mutate` (not `mutateAsync`) in the `idleMutation` stub, because at the time the tests were written `mutate` was the API. When the component switched to `mutateAsync`, the tests continued to pass because both were in the stub — masking the contract change.

The deeper issue: the component's observable contract from a test perspective is "fires the mutation when authenticated and not yet attempted." But the test verifies `mockMutate.toHaveBeenCalledWith('myspecialtoken')` — an implementation detail (which function was called) rather than the observable behavior (the API request was made). The Playwright test is more contract-oriented: it verifies the navigation happened, which is the true externally-observable outcome.

**Why hard to debug:** When `mutate` was replaced by `mutateAsync`, the RTL tests didn't break. The tests gave false confidence that the component was correct. The Playwright test caught the actual failure, but by then the RTL "evidence" had already consumed debugging time eliminating component logic as the cause.

**Cost:** This design contributed to every session from 16 onwards. The false-green RTL tests directed debugging attention away from the component's async state management and toward infrastructure (seed endpoint, auth state, API responses).

## 2. Reference Guide: Writing Playwright + RTL Tests for This Stack

---

### Rule 1: Always render Fluent UI typography with `as="h1/h2/..."` to get ARIA roles
**Anti-pattern:**
```tsx
<Title1>Accept Invitation</Title1>  // renders as <span> — no heading role
```
**Pattern:**
```tsx
<Title1 as="h1">Accept Invitation</Title1>  // renders as <h1> — getByRole('heading') works
```
**Why:** Fluent UI `Title1`, `Title2`, `Body1`, etc. default to `<span>` elements. `getByRole('heading')` finds nothing. Visual output is identical; only the accessibility tree differs. WCAG 2.1 AA requires proper heading structure regardless.

**Applies to:** All Fluent UI typography components in the codebase. Verify with `getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })` in every component test — if it fails with no other obvious reason, check the `as` prop.

---

### Rule 2: Explicitly apply `role="alert"` to Fluent UI MessageBar for ARIA-based locators
**Anti-pattern:**
```tsx
<MessageBar intent="error">...</MessageBar>  // no alert role exposed to ARIA tree
```
**Pattern:**
```tsx
<MessageBar intent="error" role="alert">...</MessageBar>
```
**Why:** Fluent UI `MessageBar` does not automatically set `role="alert"`. Without it, `getByRole('alert')` and `page.getByRole('alert')` return nothing. The Playwright tests' `filter({ hasText: ... })` chain only works because the explicit prop is in place. This is both a testability requirement and an accessibility requirement (live regions must be announced to screen readers).

---

### Rule 3: In RTL, mock at the hook boundary, not the fetch boundary — but verify the contract, not the implementation
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Verifies implementation detail — breaks when mutate → mutateAsync
const mockMutate = vi.fn()
mockUseAcceptInvite.mockReturnValue({ ...idleMutation, mutate: mockMutate })
// ...
expect(mockMutate).toHaveBeenCalledWith('myspecialtoken')
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
// Verifies observable contract — survives internal refactoring
const mockMutateAsync = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(acceptResponse)
mockUseAcceptInvite.mockReturnValue({ ...idleMutation, mutateAsync: mockMutateAsync })
// ...
await waitFor(() => expect(mockMutateAsync).toHaveBeenCalledWith('myspecialtoken'))
// Better yet: verify the downstream effect
await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('Home Page')).toBeInTheDocument())
```
**Why:** Component contracts are defined by what the component does (navigates to `/`), not how it does it (calls `mutate` vs `mutateAsync`). When you mock at the hook boundary but assert on internal function calls, any refactoring of the hook's API surface breaks tests without breaking behavior. The RTL "auto-calls mutation" test should assert that `navigate('/')` was called, or that the home page renders — not which function the component invoked.

---

### Rule 4: Never use `mutate` when the component needs to chain on the result; always use `mutateAsync`
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// mutate result is only available through TanStack Query's observer —
// destroyed on StrictMode fake-unmount
mutate(token)
// separate effect watching data — never fires if observer was destroyed
useEffect(() => {
  if (data) navigate('/')
}, [data, navigate])
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
// Promise chain is not tied to React observer lifecycle
mutateAsync(token)
  .then(() => navigate('/'))
  .catch(() => {}) // error already in mutation state for render
```
**Why:** React 18 StrictMode intentionally fakes an unmount+remount cycle. TanStack Query's `MutationObserver` is destroyed on the fake unmount. When the mutation resolves, it notifies the destroyed observer — the remounted component's fresh observer never receives the result. Promise `.then()` callbacks fire when the Promise resolves regardless of component lifecycle. `navigate` from React Router v6 is a stable reference that is safe to call from outside the component's effect tree.

**Rule of thumb:** Use `mutate` for fire-and-forget mutations where the UI reads state from `data`/`error` on re-render. Use `mutateAsync` when you need to chain imperative logic (navigation, conditional redirect, cascading mutation) on the mutation result.

---

### Rule 5: Always guard auto-firing `useEffect` mutations with `useRef` to survive StrictMode
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
useEffect(() => {
  mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/'))
}, [token, mutateAsync, navigate])
// Fires twice in StrictMode — second call hits already-consumed token
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
const hasAttempted = useRef(false)

useEffect(() => {
  if (hasAttempted.current) return
  if (!isUnauthenticated && token) {
    hasAttempted.current = true
    mutateAsync(token).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})
  }
}, [isUnauthenticated, token, mutateAsync, navigate])
```
**Why:** `useRef` survives StrictMode's fake unmount while state variables, `useState`, and TanStack Query mutation state do not. The guard prevents the second StrictMode effect invocation from making a second API call. Without it, one-time operations (invitation acceptance, payment processing, any idempotent-by-design endpoint) fire twice in development, consuming the resource before the success path can run.

**Important caveat:** This pattern is necessary in production code because StrictMode behavior in development mirrors unmount/remount patterns that occur legitimately in production (e.g., React Suspense boundaries, concurrent rendering). Don't disable StrictMode to avoid the issue — fix the effect.

---

### Rule 6: Auth state setup — the dev authenticate endpoint is always required for test users
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Assumes INVITEE_EMAIL can use Google OAuth
setup('authenticate as invitee', async ({ page }) => {
  setup.skip(!BYPASS, 'bypass path only')
  await page.goto(`${API_BASE}/api/v1/dev/authenticate?email=...`)
})
// Result: invitee.json is never written in demo mode
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
setup('authenticate as unregistered invitee', async ({ page }) => {
  // No Google sign-in path exists for test invitees — dev endpoint is the only option
  // regardless of whether PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS is set.
  await page.goto(`${API_BASE}/api/v1/dev/authenticate?email=${encodeURIComponent(INVITEE_EMAIL)}`)
  await page.waitForURL(`${WEB_BASE}/**`)
  await page.context().storageState({ path: INVITEE_AUTH })
})
```
**Why:** The Google OAuth path is only available for users who have real Google accounts and are added as test users in the Google Cloud Console. Test invitees and unregistered users are synthetic — they exist only in the test DB. There is no Google sign-in path for them. The dev authenticate endpoint is always the right tool for these personas, regardless of `PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS`. Only the admin setup test has a real-Google path; all other personas use the dev endpoint exclusively.

---

### Rule 7: Guard storageState setup with an existence check to avoid forced re-auth
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
setup('google: authenticate as admin', async ({ page, context }) => {
  setup.skip(BYPASS, 'real Google path only')
  // No existence check — forces re-auth on every demo run
  await page.goto(`${WEB_BASE}/signin`)
  // ... Google sign-in ...
  await context.storageState({ path: ADMIN_AUTH })
})
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
setup('google: authenticate as admin', async ({ page, context }) => {
  setup.skip(BYPASS, 'real Google path only')
  setup.skip(
    fs.existsSync(ADMIN_AUTH),
    'saved session exists — delete playwright/.auth/admin.json to force re-auth'
  )
  setup.setTimeout(180_000)
  // ... Google sign-in ...
  await context.storageState({ path: ADMIN_AUTH })
})
```
**Why:** The `setup` project runs as a dependency before every `chromium` project run. Without the existence guard, every `npm run test:e2e:demo` forces a new Google sign-in even when the saved session is still valid (Google sessions last weeks). This is a friction cost on every test run that is entirely avoidable.

---

### Rule 8: Dev seed endpoint admin lookup must use `system_role` not email
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Falls apart when admin email is the developer's real Google address
data: { adminEmail: ADMIN_EMAIL }
// ...endpoint queries by email, but ADMIN_EMAIL = 'admin@test.local' default
```
**Pattern:**
```sql
SELECT id FROM users WHERE system_role = 'Admin' LIMIT 1
```
**Why:** The seeded admin user has whatever email the developer configured in `Seed:AdminEmail` user secrets. A constant in `auth.helpers.ts` pointing to `'admin@test.local'` will never match the real seeded admin. The dev seed endpoint should discover the admin dynamically by role. Note SQLite's case-sensitive `=` operator: `'Admin'` (Pascal case, matching the migration) not `'admin'`.

---

### Rule 9: Integration test infrastructure must neutralize rate limiters
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Integration tests run against production rate limiter configuration
// 20 concurrent requests → 10 rejected with 429 → test appears to fail for wrong reason
```
**Pattern:**
```csharp
// KanbanWebAppFactory.ConfigureServices:
services.RemoveAll(typeof(IConfigureOptions<RateLimiterOptions>));
services.AddRateLimiter(opts => {
    opts.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;
    opts.AddFixedWindowLimiter("anonymous", o => { o.PermitLimit = 10_000; o.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1); });
    opts.AddSlidingWindowLimiter("authenticated", o => { o.PermitLimit = 10_000; ... });
    opts.AddSlidingWindowLimiter("mutating", o => { o.PermitLimit = 10_000; ... });
});
```
**Why:** Integration tests that exercise concurrency semantics must not have their behavior shaped by rate limiting. The test for concurrent acceptance is verifying DB-level `consumed_at IS NULL` atomicity — it should not be constrained by a 10-request/minute bucket. This is a general rule: integration tests should disable or vastly raise all infrastructure limits (rate limiter, retry budgets, timeouts) that are not themselves the subject of the test.

**Important:** Every named policy in `Program.cs` must also appear in the factory override. A missing policy causes a runtime error on any endpoint using `.RequireRateLimiting`. Add a maintenance comment to this effect in the factory.

---

### Rule 10: Component test idleMutation stub must include both `mutate` and `mutateAsync`
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
const idleMutation = {
  mutate: vi.fn(),
  // mutateAsync omitted — test breaks silently if component switches to mutateAsync
  data: undefined, error: null, isPending: false, ...
}
```
**Pattern:**
```typescript
const idleMutation = {
  mutate: vi.fn(),
  mutateAsync: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  data: undefined, error: null, isPending: false,
  isIdle: true, isSuccess: false, isError: false,
  variables: undefined, context: undefined,
  failureCount: 0, failureReason: null, isPaused: false,
  status: 'idle' as const, submittedAt: 0, reset: vi.fn(),
}
```
**Why:** The full TanStack Query mutation return type includes both. If the component uses `mutateAsync` and the test only provides `mutate`, the component calls `undefined()` and throws. TypeScript should catch this — which means the test fixture's type annotation should be `UseMutationResult<TData, TError, TVariables>`, not an inline object literal with inferred type.

---

### Rule 11: For Playwright async assertions, use `waitForResponse` to separate API timing from UI timing
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// Conflates "API call succeeded" with "navigation happened"
// Timeout message says nothing about whether the API even responded
await expect(page).toHaveURL(`${WEB_BASE}/`, { timeout: 15_000 })
```
**Pattern (for debugging; remove after fix):**
```typescript
const [acceptResponse] = await Promise.all([
  page.waitForResponse(resp => resp.url().includes('/invites/') && resp.url().endsWith('/accept')),
  page.goto(`${WEB_BASE}/accept/${token}`)
])
expect(acceptResponse.status()).toBe(200)
await expect(page).toHaveURL(`${WEB_BASE}/`, { timeout: 5_000 })
```
**Why:** `toHaveURL` timeout tells you the navigation never happened, but not why. `waitForResponse` separates the question "did the API call succeed?" from "did the navigation happen?" When these are separate, you immediately know whether the problem is in the API or in the component's response to the API. This is the diagnostic pattern used in Session 17 (`page.on('response')`) — make it the default for any test where an API call triggers a navigation.

---

### Rule 12: Test the component contract at the integration level in Playwright; test the rendering contract at the unit level in RTL
**Anti-pattern:**
```typescript
// RTL test verifies that the component calls mutate when certain state is present.
// Playwright test also verifies the same thing by checking navigation.
// → Two tests, same coverage, different failure modes, one is less trustworthy.
```
**Pattern:**
- **RTL:** Verifies rendering — "given this auth state, renders this button"; "given this error state, renders this message." Does not exercise the mutation lifecycle.
- **Playwright:** Verifies the full user journey — "user lands on /accept/token, API is called, user is navigated to /." This is the only test that exercises the `mutateAsync → .then(navigate)` path end-to-end.

**Why:** RTL with mocked hooks cannot test async mutation lifecycle (StrictMode double-fire, observer destruction on remount) because the lifecycle itself is mocked away. Playwright exercises the real component in a real browser with real React lifecycle. Don't try to duplicate Playwright's coverage in RTL — you will either mock too much (losing the value) or not enough (fighting React internals in jsdom).

**Concrete implication:** The RTL "on successful acceptance navigates to home" test is valuable for verifying that the component renders the home page when mutation state is `isSuccess: true`, but it cannot and should not try to verify that `mutateAsync` is called, returns a promise, and chains to `navigate`. Let Playwright own that.

## 3. Spec / Constitution Update Recommendations

### 3.1 Add a "Fluent UI ARIA Contract" subsection to Section IX — Non-Functional Requirements (Usability)

**Proposed addition after the existing Fluent UI 2 bullet:**

> **Fluent UI ARIA requirements (non-negotiable):**
> - All Fluent UI typography components (`Title1`–`Title3`, `Subtitle1`–`Subtitle2`) MUST be rendered with the `as` prop set to the appropriate semantic element (`"h1"`–`"h6"`) whenever they serve a structural heading purpose. Default `<span>` rendering violates WCAG 2.1 AA heading structure requirements and breaks `getByRole('heading')` locators.
> - All `MessageBar` components used for status feedback (errors, warnings, successes) MUST include `role="alert"` so screen readers announce them and `getByRole('alert')` locators work in tests.
> - The RTL test for every page/component that includes a heading MUST assert `getByRole('heading', { level: N })` — this is a WCAG AA gate, not optional coverage.

---

### 3.2 Add a "Test Infrastructure Isolation" rule to Section II — Test-Driven Development

**Proposed addition after the existing "Four test layers are required" table:**

> **Integration test infrastructure isolation (non-negotiable):**
> - `WebApplicationFactory` overrides MUST disable or raise to non-constraining levels all infrastructure rate limits, retry budgets, and timeouts that are not the direct subject of the test being written.
> - Named rate limiter policies registered in `Program.cs` MUST have corresponding permissive overrides in `KanbanWebAppFactory`. A missing policy override causes runtime errors on endpoints using `.RequireRateLimiting` — the factory MUST include a maintenance comment listing all policies requiring override.
> - Concurrency tests MUST document the exact DB invariant being verified (e.g., `consumed_at IS NULL` atomicity) and explicitly state that rate limiting and Polly budgets are set to non-constraining values for the test.

### 3.3 Add "React StrictMode and One-Shot Mutations" to the Frontend State Management section

**Proposed addition after the "Mutation Pattern" subsection:**

> **StrictMode and one-shot mutations (non-negotiable):**
> - React 18 StrictMode intentionally invokes effects twice in development (mount → fake-unmount → remount). Effects that fire `mutate()` or `mutateAsync()` for one-shot operations (invitation acceptance, payment, any endpoint that consumes a single-use resource) MUST be guarded with a `useRef(false)` guard (`hasAttempted` pattern). `useRef` survives StrictMode's fake unmount; mutation state does not.
> - When a mutation result must drive imperative navigation or a cascading action, MUST use `mutateAsync` (returns a Promise) rather than `mutate` (result only available through TanStack Query's observer). The `MutationObserver` is destroyed on StrictMode's fake unmount; a Promise chain is not. Pattern: `mutateAsync(arg).then(() => navigate('/')).catch(() => {})`.
> - Use `mutate` only for mutations where the component renders from `data`/`error` state on the next render cycle and no imperative chaining is needed.

### 3.4 Add a Playwright auth setup subsection to the E2E section in Section II — TDD

**Proposed addition in the E2E Playwright row:**

> **Playwright auth setup rules:**

> - The dev authenticate endpoint (`GET /api/v1/dev/authenticate`) is registered only in `IsDevelopment()`. Tests MUST NOT depend on it in a configuration that could run against a non-development environment.
> - `ADMIN_EMAIL` in test helpers MUST be documented as requiring the same value as `Seed:AdminEmail` user secret. Do not default to a synthetic address; instead, the dev seed endpoint MUST discover the admin by `system_role = 'Admin'` query, not by email constant.

---

### 3.5 Add a "Component Contract Testing" note to Section II — TDD (Fluent UI component test tiers)

**Proposed addition to the Fluent UI component test tiers decision tree:**

> **Tier boundary rule (prevents false-green coverage):**
> - RTL component tests verify **rendering given state**: given `isError: true` and `error.status: 410`, renders the correct `MessageBar`. They MUST mock hooks at the module boundary and assert on rendered output, not on which internal function was called.
> - RTL component tests MUST NOT attempt to verify async mutation lifecycle (StrictMode double-fire, observer destruction, Promise chaining). This lifecycle can only be verified in a real browser environment — use Playwright for this.
> - The idleMutation test fixture MUST be typed as `UseMutationResult<TData, TError, TVariables>` to catch API surface changes at test compilation time, not at test runtime.

---

## 4. PM Perspective: Signal vs Noise

### Which failures were "preventable noise" vs "valuable signal"

**Preventable noise (should never have reached debugging):**

- `[ThreadStatic]` in `TestAuthenticationHandler` — this is a known threading anti-pattern in any async .NET context. A constitution rule specifying "test authentication handlers MUST use thread-safe state storage" would have prevented one full session.
- `ADMIN_EMAIL = 'admin@test.local'` constant mismatch — this is a configuration coupling problem. The seed endpoint should never have accepted an email parameter at all; the admin should always be discovered by role.
- `auth.setup.ts` missing the `fs.existsSync` guard — this is a known Playwright setup pattern that appears in the official docs. Cost: multiple forced re-auths and session overhead.
- StrictMode double-fire without the `hasAttempted` guard — React's own documentation describes this behavior and the ref guard pattern. This is a well-known React 18 issue with a documented solution.

**Valuable signal (these failures caught real problems):**

- Rate limiter being global instead of per-IP — the integration test's concurrency failure revealed a genuine production bug. Without a 20-concurrent-request test, this would have been invisible until production traffic hit the limit.
- FK constraint enforcement change in `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite 10.0.8` — the test correctly caught that the `TryConsumeAsync` implementation had an ordering bug that was only harmless because FK enforcement was historically off by default.
- `google.missing_sub` error during real Google setup — this caught a real claim-name remapping bug in `GoogleIdentityAdapter` that would have broken every production sign-in.
- `mutateAsync` observer destruction on remount — this is a genuine React + TanStack Query interaction that the Playwright test correctly identified as broken behavior. The RTL suite was green, which gave false confidence.

**Summary:** Approximately 60% of the debugging time in Sessions 14-17 was spent on preventable noise (configuration mismatches, known framework patterns, threading anti-patterns). The remaining 40% was valuable signal that caught real production bugs.

---

### What the team should do differently at the test planning phase

**1. Write the auth setup matrix before writing any tests.**
The current `auth.helpers.ts` has three personas but the rules governing which path each persona takes (real Google vs dev endpoint, bypass-conditional vs always-dev-endpoint) are implicit. Before writing a single test, produce a table:

| Persona | Real Google path? | Bypass path? | Dev endpoint required? | Notes |
|---------|------------------|--------------|----------------------|-------|
| Admin | Yes (one-time setup) | Yes (CI) | No | Existence-guarded |
| Invitee | No | Bypass only | Always | No Google identity |
| Unregistered | No | Bypass only | Always | No Google identity |

Any deviation from this table during test writing is a red flag that requires explicit justification.

**2. Document the StrictMode contract for every component that uses `useEffect` with an API call.**
This is a one-line comment: `// One-shot: guarded by hasAttempted ref to survive StrictMode double-invoke`. Its absence in a new component is a code review trigger, not a debugging exercise.

**3. Classify component tests by what they can and cannot verify.**
RTL tests should be labelled with what they prove ("renders error state given 410 error") and what they don't prove ("does not verify that the mutation is invoked from the correct lifecycle hook"). This prevents false confidence from green RTL results when Playwright is failing.

The US3 acceptance scenarios in the spec (`specs/001-auth-onboarding/spec.md`) describe outcomes at the user-visible level but don't specify the ARIA contract. Acceptance criteria should include:

**Instead of:**
> Scenario 3 — expired token shows invitation-no-longer-valid error

**Write:**
> Scenario 3 — expired token: the page displays an error message with text matching "no longer valid" in a region with `role="alert"`. The URL remains at `/accept/<token>`. No navigation occurs.

**Instead of:**
> Scenario 1 — valid token with matching email creates registered user

**Write:**
> Scenario 1 — valid token: after Google authentication, the page auto-submits the acceptance. On success, the browser navigates to `/` within 15 seconds. The main landmark (`role="main"`) becomes visible. No user interaction is required.

This level of specificity in acceptance criteria serves three purposes: (1) it makes the Playwright locator choices deterministic — `getByRole('alert')` vs `getByText(...)` is obvious from the criterion, (2) it surfaces ARIA requirements at story-writing time rather than at code-review time, and (3) it makes the failure message from a failed assertion directly map to the acceptance criterion, reducing diagnosis time.
